supplement.holds: According to the main-text references: A contains survey measures and story-rating definitions/criteria (p. 17); B contains song-demo materials (p. 23); C contains lyric-rating definitions/criteria (p. 24); D contains further Experiment 1 supplementary-analysis details, including its omnibus model (pp. 21-22); E is cited for the Experiment 2 omnibus model (p. 29); F contains additional simple-slope figures (pp. 19-20). Exact embedding-analysis coverage and any supplementary standard errors could not be confirmed. Experiment 1 embedding results have no numeric estimates in the PDF; Experiment 2 gives coefficients and p-values but no standard errors (pp. 21, 28-29).

paper_design_summary: Two experiments randomly assigned individuals to a GPT-4 dialogue tool or no AI for creative writing. Experiment 1 analyzed 162 people recruited in China who wrote flash fiction in a lab (p. 16; Table 2, p. 41); Experiment 2 analyzed 329 lyric works from 299 people after attrition and recording-suitability selection during a one-week online task (pp. 23-24; Tables 4-8, pp. 43-47). Online panels scored novelty, usefulness, and overall impression of stories, lyric text, and recorded lyrics, with supplementary output-similarity analyses and moderation analyses using education, IQ, and domain experience (pp. 17-21, 24-29).

assignment.quote: they were randomly assigned to one of two conditions: one group used generative AI (GPT-4) to compose a flash-fiction of under 500 Chinese characters, while the other group completed the task without AI assistance.
assignment.locator: p. 16, Experiment 1, Samples and Procedures; Figure 1, p. 48

arms.description: Wrote the flash fiction with a GPT-4 chat interface built on the OpenAI API; received basic fiction-writing instructions plus guidance on prompt crafting.

participants.exclusions: No participant exclusions are reported. The text reports 162 individuals and Table 2 uses 162 observations. Arm counts at assignment and analysis are not explicitly stated. Two raters, rather than creative-task participants, were excluded for attention-check failures (p. 18). The AI-interaction subgroup counts on p. 21 do not explicitly establish the full AI-arm count.
participants.who: The analyzed sample comprised people with an interest in story creation recruited through social media and online interest groups: 101 college students and professionals from other sectors; 68.52 percent female; mean age 26.27; 95.06 percent with at least a bachelor's degree. Paid 30 CNY (p. 16).

outcomes.name: Novelty of flash fiction
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Consensual assessment technique; online panel of raters, 10-point scale; novelty = novel and distinctive ideas, originality and uniqueness; ICC2 = .90-.91; average 43.87 raters per story (SD 1.77). OLS with controls for education, IQ, specific human capital, age, gender, openness, AI use frequency, purpose for experiment, mind perception of AI, and the AI identification ratio (share of raters who believed the story used AI, a rater judgment made after treatment). Robust SEs. Omnibus model with all interactions in online Appendix D. Alternative AI Use coefficients from Models 2a, 2b, and 3 are 0.382, 0.361, 0.386, respectively (p. 41, Table 2); these are variants of the same outcome, not separate outcomes. Measurement details and ICCs: pp. 17-18.

assignment.what_was_assigned: GPT-4 assistance versus no AI support for lyric writing. Participants also received an assigned song demo, but random allocation of demos is not stated. Lyric-writing experience was measured, not randomized (pp. 23, 25-26; Figure 2, p. 49).
assignment.quote: After registration and an online IQ test (Nstart = 685), participants were randomly assigned to either an AI-assisted group or a control group that composed lyrics without AI support.
assignment.locator: p. 23, Experiment 2, Sample and Procedures; Figure 2, p. 49

arms.name: AI-assisted group
arms.description: Wrote lyrics with the GPT-4 chat interface; basic lyric-writing instructions plus guidance on using generative AI.

arms.name: Control (no AI)
arms.description: Wrote lyrics without AI support; basic lyric-writing instructions.

participants.exclusions: The paper labels 685 as Nstart after registration and an online IQ test (p. 23), but does not explicitly confirm the number randomized. It reports Ninformation = 611, Nsubmission = 348, and a 43.04% dropout rate during lyric creation. The analyzed sample comprised 329 works from 299 participants whose submissions producers and singers deemed suitable for recording; 289 of these analyzed participants wrote only one song (96.66%) (p. 24). Regressions analyze the 329 works (Tables 4-8, pp. 43-47). Arm-specific assignment, analysis, and attrition counts are not stated. The AI-interaction subgroup counts on p. 28 do not explicitly establish the full AI-arm count.
participants.who: Recruited from universities, companies, and online music platforms, including novices and people with lyric-writing/publication experience (pp. 22-23). The 299 analyzed participants had mean age 24.10, 63.88% were female, and 93.31% held at least a bachelor's degree (p. 24). Completion was incentivized with 100 CNY and a professionally recorded song (p. 23). The prior-publication response distribution reports 64.44% answering No, with no explicit unique-person denominator for that percentage (pp. 25-26).
participants.quote: Among the submissions, 329 works from 299 participants were deemed suitable for song recording by professional producers and singers.
participants.locator: pp. 22-24, Experiment 2, Sample and Procedures; pp. 25-26, Specific human capital; pp. 43-44, Tables 4-5, Observations rows

ai_tool.name_model: GPT-4 via the OpenAI API, in a dialogue-based interface built by the authors (same tool as Experiment 1)
ai_tool.how_used: Participants used the GPT-4 dialogue interface during the online lyric-writing task, which allowed one week at their own pace; the AI group received additional generative-AI guidance. The physical location of writing is not stated (pp. 15-16, 23).

task.description: Write lyrics for an assigned song demo consisting of instrumental accompaniment and a vocal melody sung with la-la-la syllables, using a simplified score with lyric breaks and suggested word counts. After the initial assignment, participants were encouraged to write for the remaining nine demos. Trained university-choir singers performed the selected lyrics, and a professional producer finalized the recordings (pp. 23-25).
task.duration: One week online, at the participant's own pace (p. 23).

outcomes.name: Similarity of lyrics (embedding cosine similarity; L2 distance)
outcomes.measure_detail: Supplementary textual embedding analysis with cosine-similarity and L2-distance variants, retained as one outcome (pp. 28-29). The paper reports increased similarity among AI-assisted outputs but does not define the compared outputs, aggregation, embedding model, observation unit, regression specification, or uncertainty method. Experiment 2 analyzed 329 works from 299 participants, some with multiple works (p. 24). The source therefore does not establish whether the analysis compares different people as required for diversity/across_people. Construct, question, and the direction expressed as creativity or between-person diversity are null pending the comparison-pool definition and participant-linked analysis code. Higher cosine similarity and lower L2 distance indicate more similar outputs; this raw result is retained. No numerical SE, analysis N, confidence interval, arm mean, or arm SD is reported (pp. 28-29). The diversity_detail strings are left empty while diversity classification is unresolved. The cited online appendices are absent, and the OSF API and printed OSF page could not be accessed during final review on 2026-10-09.

contrasts.reported: Cosine: b = 0.014, p = .008; L2 distance: b = -0.014, p = .007. The paper reports increased similarity among AI-assisted outputs. No SE, N, arm means, or arm SDs are printed. A direction for between-person diversity is not assigned because the comparison pool is unconfirmed. The p_value_only availability flag denotes the lack of a reported SE; the printed coefficients are retained here.

eligibility.reason: Both experiments independently meet all three core criteria. Individuals were randomly assigned to GPT-4 assistance versus no AI (p. 16, Experiment 1, Samples and Procedures; p. 23, Experiment 2, Sample and Procedures). Experiment 1 analyzed 162 people (p. 16; Table 2, p. 41); Experiment 2 analyzed 299 people contributing 329 works after attrition and recording-suitability selection (p. 24; Tables 4-8, pp. 43-47). Online panels rated novelty and usefulness of the produced stories, lyrics, and recorded lyrics (p. 17; pp. 24-25). GPT-4 was available during production in the treatment arms (pp. 16-17, 23). The unresolved comparison pool for the supplementary lyric-similarity outcome S2-O7 does not affect criterion 3 because the external novelty and usefulness ratings qualify independently. Exact randomized and arm-specific counts, attrition by arm, and the other open items do not leave any of the three criteria uncertain.

one_line_finding: With GPT-4 available, flash-fiction novelty increased (b = 0.403, SE 0.19, p = .035; p. 19 and Table 2, p. 41), lyric novelty showed no clear difference (b = 0.087, SE 0.11; Table 4, p. 43), and the paper reported higher lyric-output similarity (cosine b = 0.014, p = .008; p. 29), with the between-person comparison basis unconfirmed.
open_questions: Exact randomized counts and arm sizes are not explicitly reported; 685 is Nstart after registration/IQ testing, not an unambiguous randomized count (pp. 16, 23-24). Attrition by arm in Experiment 2 is unavailable.
Experiment 2 recruitment country and participants' physical writing locations are not stated (pp. 22-24).

Online Appendices A-F are outside this PDF and OSF access failed. Exact supplement location/content, Experiment 1 similarity estimates, and embedding methods/units/precision for both experiments remain unconfirmed (pp. 1, 17, 19-24, 28-29).
Figure 4 gives the low-education slope p = 0.068 (p. 51), whereas the corresponding text gives p = .968 (p. 19). The correct p-value cannot be settled from this document.
No unadjusted arm means or treatment models omitting the post-treatment rater AI-identification ratio are printed (pp. 19, 26; Tables 1-8).
Experiment 2 has multiple outputs from some people; its tables report robust SEs without a stated participant-clustering adjustment (p. 24; Tables 4-8).
No participant-sharing statement confirms overlap with other papers or between the experiments; the broader-project footnote is not a sample-overlap declaration (p. 16).

For S2-O7, do the similarity calculations compare outputs from different people, and how are multiple works by the same person handled? The analyzed lyric sample has 329 works from 299 people (p. 24), and the comparison pool is not defined (pp. 28-29). Construct, question, and diversity direction remain null pending confirmation from participant-linked data and analysis code.
notes: All 103217 characters of the markdown conversion were read in consecutive chunks, including references, tables, and the final figure pages. The 53-page PDF ends with Figures 7-8 and contains no online appendices. PDF page numbers equal printed page numbers. Main estimates, descriptive statistics, interaction coefficients, counts, and rating details were checked with PyMuPDF page text; the figure images were inspected directly in memory. All 11 outcomes common to A and B are retained; robustness variants are not separate outcomes. Self-reported ownership/self-efficacy and process measures are excluded. The two similarity-analysis unit fields and the ambiguous Experiment 2 randomized count were corrected from the shared raw-form assumptions to null. The lyric-only overall-quality construct was corrected from other to usefulness under the codebook. The song-rating scale is not separately confirmed. Timing refers to production of the scored creative output: the one-week online writing period and subsequent recording do not constitute an unassisted after-AI assessment. Primary status is not stated for the main ratings; embedding analyses are supplementary. The main coefficients condition on the post-treatment AI-identification ratio. Additional source inconsistencies: p. 20 cites Figure 6 for usefulness slopes 0.706 and -0.065, but Figure 6 (p. 52) is labeled novelty and prints 0.605 (p = 0.012) and 0.166 (p = 0.514); p. 26 cites Figure 7 for a lyric-novelty slope 0.389, but Figure 7 (p. 53) is explicitly a song-rating plot with slopes 0.241 (p = 0.016) and 0.033 (p = 0.732). The p. 26 simple-slope text prints t(308) despite 329 regression observations; it is not recalculated here. No effect sizes or missing SEs were computed. Reconciliation difference counts concern substantive differences between raw forms; shared facts that could not be confirmed are separately recorded in agreed_fields_checked and open_questions. Final review on 2026-10-09 independently covered the full markdown, checked the eligibility and challenged passages with PyMuPDF page text, verified the retained numerical results against PDF Tables 1-8 and Results passages, and inspected Figures 1-8 from PDF renderings in memory. S1-O3 is now usefulness because the authors explicitly describe it as story quality. The S2-O7 challenge remains open: unsupported diversity/across_people and diversity-direction codes were cleared to null, while the printed similarity coefficients and p-values were retained. Its method details are recorded in measure_detail pending construct confirmation. One challenge is corrected and one is open; there are no eligibility-affecting open items. The original reconciliation object is preserved unchanged as a record of the earlier review; the final object records the current decisions. No effect sizes or missing statistics were calculated.
